lead: Ethereum is a public blockchain that keeps a shared record of accounts, not a list of coins. Thousands of computers called nodes run client software, check every transaction, and agree on one world state: a table of accounts holding balances, code and storage. Around the network sits an ecosystem — wallets that hold keys, block explorers that show history, testnets for free practice, and applications that use it. This chapter maps the network, account model and ecosystem, then points forward to ether, the EVM and contracts.
prereq: You need: blockchain networks and nodes (Unit 1, Blockchain networks and nodes) and peer-to-peer networking (Unit 3, Peer-to-peer networking: architecture and network discovery).

blocks.text: Ethereum is public and permissionless. There is no application form or approving administrator. Any computer running the right software can join, download the chain, verify it, and pass on new transactions.

A node is such a computer. The program it runs is a client. After proof of stake, a node normally runs two clients: an execution client that keeps account state and runs contract code, and a consensus client that follows the fork-choice rule for new blocks. Both are needed for full validation.

Nodes find each other peer-to-peer. No central server is involved. A node keeps a list of peers and exchanges new transactions, new blocks, and requests for state it does not hold. Many nodes repeat the same checks, so one lying node is ignored.

A full node answers 'what is this balance now'. An archive node also answers 'what was this balance at block 15,000,000'. A light node asks a full node for the value plus a Merkle proof, and checks that the proof hashes up to the state root inside a header it already holds. Running your own full node is the strongest way to stop trusting someone else's server.
Ethereum stores accounts, not coins. That is the main structural difference from Bitcoin, which tracks unspent outputs. An account is a record with four fields:

items: nonce — the number of transactions this account has sent (for a contract account, the number of contracts it has created).
balance — ether held, counted in wei; 1 ETH = 10¹⁸ wei.
codeHash — the hash of the account's code; for an externally owned account it is the Keccak-256 hash of empty code (the same fixed value for every EOA).
storageRoot — the root hash of the account's own storage.

blocks.text: There are two account types. An externally owned account (EOA) is controlled by a private key and carries no code. A contract account carries code and is controlled by that code. Making a wallet creates an EOA; deploying a contract creates a contract account.

The world state is the whole table of address → account. Every full node that has validated the chain holds the same table; light nodes keep only headers and fetch values with proofs. Each block header carries a 32-byte state root, a fingerprint of the entire table (see Unit 2, Merkle trees). Two nodes that disagree on any balance get different roots, so disagreement is visible immediately.
new balance = balance − value − gasUsed × effectiveGasPrice
blocks.where: balance is the sender's balance in wei before the transaction; value is the wei sent to the recipient; gasUsed is the gas actually consumed; effectiveGasPrice is the price of one gas unit in wei, equal to base fee + priority fee. The product gasUsed × effectiveGasPrice is the fee. The whole fee leaves the sender and never reaches the recipient: the base fee is burned, and only the priority fee goes to the block producer.

blocks.text: The nonce orders one account's transactions and blocks replay: a signed transaction with nonce 7 is valid once only, because afterwards the account's nonce is 8. Transaction fields are covered in 5.2.
The core chain is small. The ecosystem is the software people actually touch:

items: Wallet — holds private keys, signs transactions, displays balances it reads from a node.
Block explorer — a search engine over the chain; look up an address, a transaction hash or a block number.
dApp — a web front end that reaches contracts through a wallet and a node.
Token — a contract keeping its own table of holder amounts; see 5.2.
Testnet — a separate chain with free ether for practice; see 5.6.
Developer tools — compilers, libraries and frameworks that build and deploy contracts; see 5.7.

blocks.text: Here is the full path of one request:

items: The user asks the wallet to send 0.3 ETH to a contract.
The wallet builds a transaction, shows the fee, and the user signs it with the private key.
The wallet sends the signed transaction to one node.
That node checks the signature, nonce and balance, then gossips the transaction to peers.
A block producer includes it; every node executes it and updates world state; the wallet refreshes by querying again.

blocks.text: A wallet is neither a chain nor a node. It is a key holder plus a viewer. If its node is stale, the wallet shows a stale number; the chain's state did not move. The node and world state decide balances and nonces, never the wallet.

figure.caption: A request moves from the user's keys to a wallet, to one node, out to peers, and ends as a change in the shared world state. Notice that the wallet only signs; the node and the state it holds decide every number.

spec.title: Ethereum ecosystem path
spec.aria: A user signs a request in a wallet, sends it to an Ethereum node, which gossips it to peer nodes and updates the shared world state.

examples.question: A wallet shows 2 ETH for an account whose nonce is 7. The user sends 0.3 ETH to a contract account and pays a gas fee of 0.001 ETH. The contract already holds 0 ETH and does nothing else during the call. Find the user's balance, the contract's balance and the user's nonce after the transaction is included in a block.
steps: Start: user balance = 2 ETH, user nonce = 7, contract balance = 0 ETH.
Value moved: 0.3 ETH leaves the user's balance and enters the contract's balance.
Fee paid: gasUsed × effectiveGasPrice = 0.001 ETH leaves the user's balance; the base fee is burned and the priority fee goes to the block producer, not the contract.
examples.answer: User balance = 1.699 ETH, contract balance = 0.3 ETH, user nonce = 8.
examples.check:
balance = 2.0
nonce = 7
value = 0.3
gas_fee = 0.001
user = balance - value - gas_fee
contract = 0.0 + value
print(round(user, 3))
print(round(contract, 3))
print(nonce + 1)

traps: Treating the wallet as the blockchain. The wallet holds keys and displays a view; the node and world state hold the truth.
Mixing up node and client. The client is the software; the node is the computer running it. Exam answers that say 'a client is a machine' lose marks.
Adding the gas fee to the receiving contract. Only the value reaches the contract; the whole fee leaves the sender, with the base fee burned and only the priority fee going to the block producer.
Forgetting the nonce goes up by exactly one per included transaction, even if the call fails during execution.
Assuming a light node keeps the full state. It keeps headers and checks proofs; the state lives on full and archive nodes.

quiz.q: Name the two clients a full Ethereum node runs today and state the job of each.
quiz.a: An execution client, which keeps account state and executes contract code, and a consensus client, which follows the proof-of-stake fork-choice rule for new blocks.

quiz.q: List the four fields of an Ethereum account.
Why does every block header carry a state root?
quiz.a: The state root is a fingerprint of the entire account table. Any node that computes a different table gets a different root, so disagreement on a single balance is detected at once.

quiz.q: Why is a wallet not the blockchain, even though it shows balances?
quiz.a: The wallet stores private keys and signs transactions. It reads balances from a node. Deleting the wallet loses keys, not funds on the chain; a stale node makes the wallet show a stale number while the chain is unchanged.

quiz.q: An account has balance 5 ETH and nonce 12. It sends 1.2 ETH to a contract and pays a gas fee of 0.004 ETH. Find the new balance and nonce.
quiz.a: Balance = 5 − 1.2 − 0.004 = 3.796 ETH. Nonce = 12 + 1 = 13. The fee does not go to the contract.

quiz.q: You must build a block explorer that answers 'what was this address's balance at block 15,000,000'. Which node type do you run and why?
quiz.a: An archive node. A full node keeps only recent state, so old balances are not directly available; an archive node keeps every historical state.

quiz.q: A light node reports a balance that differs from an archive node's answer. Give two possible causes and how you would check each.
quiz.a: First, the light node may be on a different chain or behind a fork, so compare block hashes and state roots at the same height. Second, the peer it queried may have answered wrongly, so verify the returned value against the state root in the header the light node already holds.

quiz.q: Why does Ethereum's account model need a nonce per account, while Bitcoin's unspent-output model does not?
quiz.a: In an account model a signed transaction is valid whenever the signature and balance fit, so an identical transaction could be replayed. The nonce makes each transaction usable once and fixes its order. Bitcoin instead marks specific unspent outputs as spent, so replay fails on the output set.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most industry teams never run a node; they rent access from a node provider that exposes the same JSON-RPC calls, billed per request. The split between execution and consensus clients keeps shifting as the protocol is upgraded, and the 'modular client' literature studies that boundary. Search 'execution client vs consensus client', 'JSON-RPC eth_getBalance' or 'stateless Ethereum' to go further. Statelessness research aims at nodes that validate without storing the whole world state, which would make light clients truly verify.
